A B S T R A C T
Rationale
Calcium supplementation may reduce the risk of developing pre-eclampsia, a common cause of serious maternal and neonatal morbidity
and death. However, its efectiveness in preventing hypertensive disorders of pregnancy is uncertain. This updates a review last published
in 2018.
Objectives
To assess the efects of calcium supplementation during pregnancy on hypertensive disorders of pregnancy and related maternal and child
outcomes.
Search methods
We searched CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, four other databases and two trials registries to 7 January 2025, and screened reference lists
of retrieved studies and relevant systematic reviews.
Eligibility criteria
We included randomised controlled trials (RCTs) that compared calcium supplementation during pregnancy with placebo or standard care
only. We compared low and high doses. Trials conducted afer 2010 had to be prospectively registered. We assessed trustworthiness.
Outcomes
Critical outcomes were pre-eclampsia for women and perinatal loss for children.
Important outcomes for women included maternal death, maternal death or severe morbidity, adverse efects and preterm delivery before
37 weeks. Important outcomes for children were neonatal death or severe morbidity, stillbirth, and neonatal death.
Risk of bias
We assessed risk of bias in RCTs using version 2 of the Cochrane tool (RoB 2).
Synthesis methods
Two review authors independently selected trials, extracted data, and assessed bias and trustworthiness. We pooled data using random-
efects meta-analysis. We assessed certainty of evidence using GRADE.

Included studies
We included 10 RCTs with 37,504 participants. All trials provided standard care. Eight compared calcium supplementation to placebo, and
two compared low- to high-dose calcium supplementation.
We excluded 20 previously included trials; 11 because eligibility criteria changed and nine because they are awaiting classification due to
trustworthiness issues.
Synthesis of results
Calcium supplementation versus placebo
Calcium may result in little to no diference in pre-eclampsia (risk ratio (RR) 0.83, 95% confidence interval (CI) 0.67 to 1.04; 6 RCTs, 15,364
women; risk diference (RD) 9/1000 fewer, 95% CI 17 fewer to 2 more; low-certainty evidence). Sensitivity analysis excluding small studies
(fewer than 500 participants) indicates little to no diference in pre-eclampsia (RR 0.92, 95% CI 0.79 to 1.05; 4 RCTs, 14,730 women; high-
certainty evidence).
The evidence is very uncertain about the efect of calcium on maternal death (RR 0.33, 95% CI 0.06 to 1.83; 3 RCTs, 9430 women; very low-
certainty evidence) and on adverse efects (RR 2.16, 95% CI 0.43 to 10.78; 2 RCTs, 714 women; very low-certainty evidence).
Calcium probably results in little to no diference in the composite outcome maternal death or severe morbidity (RR 0.80, 95% CI 0.54 to
1.19; 1 RCT, 8312 women; moderate-certainty evidence), and may result in little to no diference in perinatal loss (RR 0.93, 95% CI 0.64 to
1.35; 4 RCTs, 6832 women; RD 1/1000 fewer, 95% CI 6 fewer to 6 more; low-certainty evidence).
The evidence is very uncertain about the efect of calcium on preterm delivery before 37 weeks (RR 0.83, 95% CI 0.65 to 1.05; 6 RCTs, 15,074
women; very low-certainty evidence). Sensitivity analysis excluding small studies indicates little to no diference in preterm delivery before
37 weeks (RR 0.97, 95% CI 0.85 to 1.11; 4 RCTs, 14,429 women; high-certainty evidence).
Calcium probably results in little to no diference in stillbirth (RR 0.91, 95% CI 0.72 to 1.15; 4 RCTs, 14,085 women; moderate-certainty
evidence) but the evidence is very uncertain about its efect on neonatal death (RR 1.09, 95% CI 0.50 to 2.38; 4 RCTs, 13,300 women; very
low-certainty evidence).
No trials measured neonatal death or severe morbidity.
Low- versus high-dose calcium
There may be little to no diference between low- and high-dose calcium in pre-eclampsia (RR 0.96, 95% CI 0.73 to 1.25; 2 RCTs, 22,000
women; low-certainty evidence).
The evidence is very uncertain about the efect of low- versus high-dose calcium on maternal death (RR 1.20, 95% CI 0.36 to 3.94; 2 RCTs,
22,000 women; very low-certainty evidence).
There is little to no diference between low- and high-dose calcium in perinatal loss (RR 1.02, 95% CI 0.91 to 1.16; 2 RCTs, 21,412 women;
high-certainty evidence), and stillbirth (RR 0.99, 95% CI 0.84 to 1.16; 2 RCTs, 21,131 women; high-certainty evidence).
There is probably little to no diference between low- and high-dose calcium in preterm delivery before 37 weeks (RR 0.98, 95% CI 0.81 to
1.17; 2 RCTs, 20,578 women; moderate-certainty evidence).
No trials measured maternal death or severe morbidity, adverse efects, neonatal death or severe morbidity, or neonatal death.
Authors' conclusions
Calcium supplementation versus placebo
Meta-analyses showed that calcium supplementation compared to placebo may result in little to no diference in pre-eclampsia, but we
are very uncertain about its efect on preterm delivery before 37 weeks. However, high-certainty evidence from sensitivity analyses with
only large trials (> 95% of participants in the main analyses), showed little to no diference in both pre-eclampsia and preterm delivery
before 37 weeks. Maternal death was rare, so evidence about it is very uncertain.
Calcium supplementation probably results in little to no diference in the composite outcome maternal death or severe morbidity, may
result in little to no diference in perinatal loss, and probably results in little to no diference in stillbirth. Evidence about adverse efects
and neonatal death is very uncertain.
No trials measured neonatal death or severe morbidity.
Baseline calcium intake level and pre-eclampsia risk status did not impact our findings.

Low- versus high-dose calcium supplementation
Low- compared to high-dose calcium supplementation made no diference to outcomes in women at high risk for pre-eclampsia in low
calcium-intake populations. Low-dose calcium supplementation may result in little to no diference in pre-eclampsia. Maternal death (5
per 10,000 women) was rare; the evidence is very uncertain. Low-dose calcium results in little to no diference in perinatal loss and stillbirth,
and probably results in little to no diference in preterm delivery before 37 weeks. No trials measured severe maternal morbidity, neonatal
death, severe neonatal morbidity, or adverse efects.

P L A I N   L A N G U A G E   S U M M A R Y
Is taking calcium supplements during pregnancy an efective way to prevent blood pressure disorders and related problems?
Key messages
•
We found little to no diference in the number of women developing pre-eclampsia when they were given calcium during pregnancy,
and we are uncertain about poor outcomes for mothers and babies.
•
Most participants started calcium in the middle 3 months of pregnancy, so we don't have information in this review about the
efectiveness of calcium supplementation in very early pregnancy. We don't have information about women with enough calcium in
their diet versus those who do not, nor those who are at high risk versus low risk of getting pre-eclampsia.
•
We found good evidence when we analysed only large studies, with more than 500 women. It is unlikely that further research would
change the current evidence. Therefore, in future, research could focus on other ways to prevent blood pressure disorders during
pregnancy.
Why is high blood pressure a problem during pregnancy?
High blood pressure in pregnancy is a leading cause of death and severe illness in mothers and babies. Pre-eclampsia is the most serious
complication. It afects the placenta and can afect other organs, such as the kidneys, liver and brain. There is currently no treatment for
pre-eclampsia apart from delivering the baby.
How might calcium help?
Some evidence suggests that calcium can lower blood pressure in people whose blood pressure is normal and in women who have had pre-
eclampsia before, but other evidence does not support this. However, calcium is readily available, cheap and likely to be safe for mothers
and babies. Calcium tablets are taken orally (swallowed). If calcium can prevent pre-eclampsia, it may reduce death and severe illness in
mothers and babies.
What did we want to find out?
We wanted to know whether calcium is efective in preventing pre-eclampsia and other high blood pressure disorders when taken during
pregnancy, and if it causes unwanted efects. We were also interested in whether calcium reduces the number of babies who die during or
soon afer birth, the number of mothers and babies who died or became ill, and babies who were born early.
What did we do?
We searched for studies that investigated calcium supplements during pregnancy. We used a checklist to make sure we only included
studies that we could trust. We made judgements about the quality of the studies before comparing and summarising their results. Lastly,
we rated our confidence in the findings.
What did we find?
We found 10 studies with 37,504 women that looked at the efects of calcium supplementation alongside standard care. Eight studies
compared calcium supplementation to placebo (a dummy treatment), and two compared low-dose (500 mg daily) to high-dose (1500 mg
daily) calcium supplementation. Studies took place worldwide, in high- and low-income countries. Some women in the studies had enough
calcium in their diets and others did not. Some women were at high risk of pre-eclampsia and others weren't.

Calcium compared to placebo (8 studies, 15,504 women)
Evidence from 6 studies (15,364 women) showed that calcium may make little to no diference to pre-eclampsia compared to placebo.
However, when we analysed only large studies with more than 500 women (4 studies, 14,730 women), we found strong evidence confirming
that calcium makes little to no diference to pre-eclampsia compared to placebo.
Calcium probably results in little to no diference in the overall risk of a mother dying or developing severe complications of pre-eclampsia.
It may result in little to no diference in death of the baby during pregnancy and early life.
We are very uncertain about the efect of calcium on the risk of mothers dying, on birth before 37 weeks, and also on unwanted efects.
Low- compared to high-dose calcium (2 studies, 22,000 women)
A lower dose of calcium may make little to no diference to pre-eclampsia compared to a higher dose. We are very uncertain about the
efect of low-dose calcium on mothers dying compared to a higher dose. Taking a lower dose makes no diference to loss of the baby during
pregnancy and early life, and probably makes little to no diference to birth before 37 weeks.
What are the limitations of the evidence?
Because most participants started calcium in the middle 3 months of pregnancy, we do not have information in this review about the
efectiveness of calcium supplementation in very early pregnancy. This is the same for women who live in areas where people have enough
calcium in their diet versus those who do not, and those who are at high risk versus low risk of getting pre-eclampsia.
How up to date is this evidence?
The evidence is current to January 2025.

B A C K G R O U N D
Description of the condition
Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy are a leading cause of
maternal and perinatal morbidity and mortality. They are
characterised by high blood pressure during pregnancy. The main
types include chronic hypertension, gestational hypertension,
pre-eclampsia, and pre-eclampsia superimposed on chronic
hypertension. Of these, pre-eclampsia is the most severe [1].
Pre-eclampsia is a multi-organ, pregnancy-specific condition
characterised by hypertension with end-organ injury. It is
associated with varying degrees of impaired placental perfusion,
which results in the release of placental factors into the maternal
circulation, causing widespread endothelial injury [1].
Pre-eclampsia is estimated to complicate about 3% to 8% of
all pregnancies [2, 3], and is estimated to cause at least 42,000
maternal deaths and more than half a million perinatal deaths
every year [2, 4, 5]. It is a progressive disease of pregnancy. The
definition has evolved over time and the majority of international
guidelines have moved to a broader classification. Most agree
that pre-eclampsia can be diagnosed as new-onset hypertension
(sustained systolic blood pressure ≥ 140 mmHg or diastolic blood
pressure ≥ 90 mmHg) with proteinuria (1+ by dipstick testing, ≥ 300
mg per 24 hours, or ≥ 30 mg/dL) [6], or end-organ dysfunction that
develops afer 20 weeks of gestation. Superimposed pre-eclampsia
is diagnosed when there is loss of blood pressure control with
worsening proteinuria, or end organ involvement.
End-organ involvement includes eclampsia (generalised seizures);
pulmonary oedema; haemolysis, elevated liver enzymes and low
platelet (HELLP) syndrome; liver dysfunction or rupture; renal
impairment; and uteroplacental involvement.
There is currently no treatment for pre-eclampsia apart from
delivery. Pre-eclampsia is therefore ofen associated with medically
induced preterm birth. Preterm survivors are at high risk
of significant morbidity, especially respiratory disease and its
sequelae, and long-term neurological morbidity [7].
Description of the intervention and how it might work
Calcium supplementation is an oral dietary supplement, usually
produced in the form of calcium carbonate or calcium gluconate.
The dose is expressed in terms of the amount of elemental calcium
in the preparation. The daily dietary calcium requirement is 1000
mg to 1200 mg.
Fify per cent of the global population are at risk of
calcium deficiency, particularly in Africa and Asia [8]. Calcium
supplementation reduces blood pressure in normotensive people
[9], and in non-pregnant women with previous pre-eclampsia [10].
An inverse relationship between calcium intake and hypertensive
disorders of pregnancy was first described in 1980 [11]. This
was based on the observation that Mayan Indians in Guatemala,
who traditionally soaked their corn in lime before cooking, had
a high calcium intake and a low incidence of pre-eclampsia and
eclampsia. A very low prevalence of pre-eclampsia had been
reported from Ethiopia, where the diet, among other features,
contained high levels of calcium [12]. These observations were
supported by other epidemiological and clinical studies, and led to
the hypothesis that an increase in calcium intake during pregnancy
might reduce the incidence of pre-eclampsia among women with
low calcium intake [13, 14, 15, 16, 17].
Low calcium intake may cause hypertension by stimulating
either parathyroid hormone or renin release, thereby increasing
intracellular calcium in vascular smooth muscle, and leading
to vasoconstriction [13]. A possible mode of action for calcium
supplementation is that it reduces parathyroid release and
intracellular calcium, and so reduces smooth muscle contractility.
By a similar mechanism, calcium supplementation could also
reduce uterine smooth muscle contractility and prevent preterm
labour and delivery [18]. Calcium might also have an indirect efect
on smooth muscle function by increasing magnesium levels [19].
Calcium supplementation is attractive as a potential intervention
to reduce the risk of developing pre-eclampsia as it is readily
available, and is likely to be safe for the woman and her child.
Why it is important to do this review
Calcium supplementation has been tested in several randomised
trials, commencing in the late 1980s, which suggested a promising
beneficial efect on hypertensive disorders and related problems.
The first systematic reviews highlighted the need for larger trials
to assess the efects on important clinical outcomes in addition
to pre-eclampsia and preterm delivery, such as perinatal mortality
[20, 21]. A subsequent systematic review came to more promising
conclusions [22], but these findings were not confirmed by a large
trial in the USA [23], and the discrepancy elicited discussion [24].
Subsequently, a large trial conducted in communities with
low dietary calcium intake also did not show that calcium
supplementation decreased the incidence of pre-eclampsia but did
report a decrease in a composite maternal adverse outcome [25].
However, this outcome had not been prespecified.
In 2018, an updated Cochrane review showed that calcium
supplementation of at least 1000 mg reduced the risk of pre-
eclampsia compared to placebo [26]. Women with adequate
dietary calcium were the only subgroup where the confidence
interval crossed the line of no efect. The authors cautioned that the
meta-analysis may be an over-estimate, as funnel plot asymmetry
suggested a small-study efect or publication bias, or both [26].
A sensitivity analysis of this Cochrane review was published in 2024
to examine the impact of study size. When the three largest studies
were assessed, which accounted for 88% of total recruitment, the
mean risk ratio was 0.92 with no significant diference [27]. There

We applied the TRACT checklist to all eligible full texts to assess
trustworthiness [37]. This checklist contains 19 items categorised
into seven domains.
•
Domain 1. Governance: included checking for absent or
retrospective registration of RCTs commencing afer 2010, as
well as absent or vague descriptions of research ethics or other
apparent concerns regarding ethics.
•
Domain 2. Author group: included checking whether authors'
other studies have been retracted, not at their request, whether
there are a large number of RCTs published in a short time frame

authors is three or fewer, or there is low author-to-study-size
ratio.
•

checking whether there were insuficient or implausible
descriptions or unnecessary or illogical description of
methodological standards.
•
Domain 4. Time frame: includes checking for fast recruitment
of participants within the study time, or short or impossible
time frames between the end of recruitment, and follow-up and
submission of the paper. The recruitment time frame is from
the date of the first recruited participant to the date of the last
recruited participant.
•
Domain 5. Dropout rates: includes checking for zero
participants lost to follow-up or for no reasons given for loss
to follow-up, especially in studies with long follow-up, as well
as an ideal number of losses to follow-up resulting in perfectly
rounded numbers in each group.

Domain 6. Baseline characteristics: includes checking for
baseline characteristics and whether no or fewer than five
baseline characteristics were presented, or implausible patient
characteristics judging from common sense, the literature, and
local data. We checked for perfect balance for multiple baseline
characteristics or significant or large diferences between
baseline characteristics, as well as important prognostic factors
not reported as baseline characteristics.
•
Domain 7. Outcomes: includes checking for efect sizes that
were much larger than in other RCTs on the same topic or
conflicting information between outcomes, as well as a change
in primary outcome from registration to publication.

Risk of bias assessment in included studies
Our review aimed to quantify the efect of assignment to the
intervention (the intention-to-treat (ITT) efect), and our risk of bias
evaluations aligned with this aim. Two review authors (CAC, CR,
ACR) assessed the risk of bias for each study independently and
in duplicate. We used version 2 of the Cochrane tool for assessing
risk of bias in randomised trials (RoB 2) [42]. We resolved any
disagreements by discussion with all the review authors.
We assessed the risk of bias for outcomes that are included in
the summary of findings tables (see Certainty of the evidence
assessment).
•
For women:
◦ pre-eclampsia;
◦ maternal death;
◦ maternal death or severe morbidity; and
◦ adverse efects.
•
For children:
◦ perinatal loss;
◦ preterm delivery before 37 weeks;
◦ neonatal death or severe morbidity;
◦ stillbirth; and
◦ neonatal death.
Detailed risk of bias assessments are available on reasonable
request.
RoB 2 assigns risk of bias judgements based on the answers to
signalling questions that fall under the following domains.
•
Bias arising from the randomisation process
•
Bias due to deviations from intended interventions
•
Bias due to missing outcome data
•
Bias in the measurement of the outcome
•
Bias in the selection of the reported result
For each outcome, we used the signalling questions to reach one of
three judgements: 'low risk of bias', 'some concerns', or 'high risk of
bias'. We used the RoB Excel tool to record answers to the signalling
questions [43]. We summarised the risk of bias judgements across
diferent studies for each of the domains for each prespecified
outcome.
The tool derives an overall judgement for each study as follows.
•
Low risk of bias: all domains have a 'low risk' judgement.
•
Some concerns: there are 'some concerns' in at least one
domain, but no domains have a 'high risk' judgement.
•
High risk of bias: at least one domain has a 'high risk' judgement,
or there are 'some concerns' in multiple domains.
Measures of treatment efect
We reported the efects of interventions for dichotomous outcomes
as risk ratios (RRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). For
continuous data, we reported mean diferences (MDs) with 95%
CIs when studies measured outcomes using the same scale. Where
results were reported in a format that could not be entered into
a meta-analysis, we used guidance provided in Chapter 6 of the
Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions to
convert the data to the necessary format [44].
For future updates of this review, we will use standardised mean
diferences for continuous outcomes if studies measure the same
outcome using diferent scales. Furthermore, where possible, we
will use outcomes adjusted for confounders or design efects
(e.g. clustering) in meta-analyses. Where studies report count
data (the number of events rather than the number of people
who experienced an event), we will use the number of events
and number of person-years to calculate rate ratios (Cochrane
Handbook section 6.7 [44]).
Unit of analysis issues
Multi-arm trials
For outcomes reported in multi-armed trials, we combined all
relevant intervention groups of the trial into a single group, and all
relevant control groups into a single control group. We combined
both the sample sizes and the numbers of people with events from
all groups for dichotomous outcomes. For continuous outcomes,
we combined means and standard deviations as per the Cochrane
Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions [45]. Where we
considered one of the arms irrelevant, we excluded it from the
analysis [45].

Cluster-randomised controlled trials
We have not identified any cluster-RCTs to date. We will include any
cluster-RCTs that we identify in future updates in the analyses along
with individually randomised trials. We will adjust their sample
sizes using the methods described in the Cochrane Handbook,
using an estimate of the intracluster correlation coeficient (ICC)

a study of a similar population [45]. If we use ICCs from other
sources, we will report this and conduct sensitivity analyses to
investigate the efect of variation in the ICC. If we identify cluster-
randomised trials in addition to the individually-randomised trials,
we plan to synthesise the relevant information. We will consider
it reasonable to combine the results from both if there is little
heterogeneity between the study designs, and we consider the
interaction between the efect of intervention and the choice of
randomisation unit to be unlikely.
Cross-over trials
Cross-over trials were not eligible for inclusion in this review.
Dealing with missing data
We contacted trial authors to verify key trial characteristics and
obtain missing numerical outcome data for trials identified as
abstract only. We reported all relevant data in the Characteristics of
included studies (Supplementary material 2). Where we made any
assumptions about missing data, we report the potential impact in
the Discussion section of the review.
As far as possible, we carried out analyses for all outcomes on an ITT
basis, that is, we attempted to include all participants randomised
to each group in the analyses, and to analyse all participants in
the group to which they had been allocated, regardless of whether
or not they received the allocated intervention. Where data were
missing because the outcome was not measured in all participants,
the reason for missing data was unrelated to the outcome, and
missing data were balanced between groups, the denominator for
each outcome in each trial was the number randomised minus any
participants whose outcomes were known to be missing (modified
ITT analysis). Where no explanation was given for missing outcome
data, missing data were not balanced between groups, and we
suspected that the missing data were related to the outcome, we
contacted the study authors and conducted sensitivity analyses.
Reporting bias assessment
We did not have suficient studies (10 or more) in the meta-analysis
to create funnel plots, but we cannot rule out the possibility of
publication bias or small-study efects.
In future updates of the review, if we include at least 10 studies in
a meta-analysis of a critical outcome (pre-eclampsia or perinatal
loss), we will create and visually inspect funnel plots and run a
formal statistical test for asymmetry to evaluate publication bias. If
we observe funnel plot asymmetry, we will discuss the implications
of reporting and non-reporting biases (e.g. small-study efects) for
our results.
Synthesis methods
We undertook meta-analyses only where this was meaningful
based on the comparability of the studies available (i.e. if the
treatments, participants and the underlying clinical question
were similar enough for pooling to make sense). We based our
choice of meta-analysis approach on an evaluation of clinical,
methodological and statistical heterogeneity. We generated pooled
analyses of outcomes with suficient data using the DerSimonian
and Laird random-efects technique [45]. We calculated the 95% CI
using the Wald-type method [45]. For random-efects analyses, we
presented the results as the average treatment efect with 95% CIs,
and the estimates of Tau2 and I2 statistics [46]. We presented the
efect estimates and 95% CIs for the individual study efects and the
pooled efect in forest plots.
For future updates of this review, we will pool data using the inverse
variance method where studies report adjusted estimates that are
appropriate to include in a meta-analysis. Where meta-analysis
is not possible, we will present results in a narrative synthesis
and create appropriate tables and figures, following the Synthesis
without meta-analysis (SWiM) reporting guideline [47].
Investigation of heterogeneity and subgroup analysis
We described the clinical diversity and methodological variability
of the evidence in the review text and with tables that present
study characteristics (design features, population characteristics,
and details of interventions). To assess statistical heterogeneity,
we visually inspected forest plots and described the direction
and magnitude of efects and the degree of 95% CI overlap.
We also considered the statistics generated in forest plots that
measure statistical heterogeneity. We used the I2 statistic to
quantify inconsistency amongst the trials in each analysis [46]. We
also considered the P value from the Chi2 test to assess whether
this heterogeneity is significant (P < 0.1). Where we identified
substantial heterogeneity, we reported the finding and explored
possible explanatory factors using prespecified subgroup analysis.
To interpret the I2 statistic value, we used the following rough
thresholds [45].
•
0% to 40%: might not be important
•
30% to 60%: may represent moderate heterogeneity
•
50% to 90%: may represent substantial heterogeneity
•
75% to 100%: considerable heterogeneity

Sensitivity analysis
Where the data showed a possibility of a small-study efect, we
performed sensitivity analysis excluding small trials. As we could
not find a definition of 'small study' in the literature, we contacted
biostatisticians and discussed this within our author team. For the
purpose of this review, we defined a small trial as one with fewer
than 500 participants. We showed the results of the sensitivity
analyses in separate forest plots and assessed the certainty of
evidence.

Certainty of the evidence assessment
Two review authors (CR, ACR) independently evaluated the
certainty of the evidence according to the five GRADE domains
(study limitations, consistency of efect, imprecision, indirectness
and publication bias) using GRADEpro GDT sofware [52], and
following the methods and recommendations provided in the
Cochrane Handbook [53]. When judging imprecision, we considered
the range of the confidence interval of the relative efect as
well as the total cumulative study population for that outcome
and the total number of events per outcome. Where there were
very few events (fewer than 30) and the confidence interval was
very wide, we downgraded for imprecision. The threshold for
suggested appreciable benefit for the relative efect was 0.75, and

Results of the search
Our database and trials register searches identified 14,903 records.
Following removal of 4154 duplicates, we excluded 3325 records
that were identified as clearly irrelevant (i.e. not RCTs) by the
Covidence automation tool.
Two review authors screened the titles and abstracts of the
remaining 7424 records, and selected 124 for comprehensive
full-text assessment. Of these, we included 10 RCTs (52
references; Supplementary material 2), and excluded 35 studies
(39 references), most commonly due to having an ineligible trial
design (Supplementary material 3). Twenty trials (31 references)
are awaiting classification (Supplementary material 4), and two
trials (2 references) are ongoing (ISRCTN12033893 2021; Oliveira
2024; Supplementary material 5). The PRISMA study flow diagram
in Figure 1 shows the results of the search process.

Included studies
Characteristics of the 10 included trials are summarised in
Supplementary material 2 and Table 1.
Participants
Ten trials (52 records) involving a total of 37,504 randomised
participants investigated the eficacy of calcium supplementation
(Belizan 1983; Belizan 1991; Crowther 1999; Dwarkanath (India)
2024; Dwarkanath (Tanzania) 2024; Goldberg 2013; Levine 1997;
Villar 1987; Villar 1990; Villar 2006). Each trial contributed the
following number of participants:
•
Belizan 1983: n = 36
•
Belizan 1991: n = 1194
•
Crowther 1999: n = 456
•
Dwarkanath (India) 2024: n = 11,000
•
Dwarkanath (Tanzania) 2024: n = 11,000
•
Goldberg 2013: n = 662
•
Levine 1997: n = 4589
•
Villar 1987: n = 52
•
Villar 1990: n = 190
•

Daily calcium intake
Three trials were conducted in populations with adequate daily
calcium intake (Levine 1997; Villar 1987; Villar 1990), and seven
trials in populations with inadequate daily calcium intake (Belizan
1983; Belizan 1991; Crowther 1999; Dwarkanath (India) 2024;
Dwarkanath (Tanzania) 2024; Goldberg 2013; Villar 2006).
Risk profile
Eight trials focused on women at high risk of pre-eclampsia (Belizan
1991; Crowther 1999; Dwarkanath (India) 2024; Dwarkanath
(Tanzania) 2024; Levine 1997; Villar 1987; Villar 1990; Villar 2006),
and two focused on women at low risk (Belizan 1983; Goldberg
2013).
Settings
Three trials were conducted in high-resource settings, including the
USA (Levine 1997; Villar 1990) and Australia (Crowther 1999).

Seven trials were conducted in lower-resource settings, including
Argentina (Belizan 1991), Guatemala (Belizan 1983), the Gambia
(Goldberg 2013), India (Dwarkanath (India) 2024)), and Tanzania
(Dwarkanath (Tanzania) 2024). A large multicentre study was
carried out in multiple countries (Villar 2006), and one trial was
conducted in the USA and Argentina (Villar 1987).
Interventions and comparisons
All included trials assessed the efects of calcium supplementation
in addition to standard care. Eight trials compared calcium
supplementation to placebo (Belizan 1983; Belizan 1991; Crowther
1999; Goldberg 2013; Levine 1997; Villar 1987; Villar 1990; Villar
2006), and two trials compared low-dose calcium supplementation
to high-dose calcium supplementation (Dwarkanath (India) 2024;
Dwarkanath (Tanzania) 2024).
Route of administration and dosage of calcium supplementation
All the trials administered calcium orally in tablet form.
Calcium versus placebo
•
Three trials administered 1500 mg calcium daily, as three 500 mg
tablets (Goldberg 2013; Villar 1987; Villar 2006).
•
Three trials administered 2000 mg calcium daily, as four 500 mg
tablets (Belizan 1991; Levine 1997; Villar 1990).
•
One three-armed trial administered 1000 mg calcium daily to
one intervention group and 2000 mg calcium daily to the other,
whilst the comparison group received identical placebo tablets.
It is unclear how many tablets each group was given daily
(Belizan 1983).
•
One trial administered 1800 mg calcium daily, as three 600 mg
tablets (Crowther 1999).
Low-dose versus high-dose calcium
•
The two trials that compared low-dose to high-dose calcium
administered 500 mg (Dwarkanath (India) 2024), and 1500 mg
(Dwarkanath (Tanzania) 2024), of calcium daily. Participants
were given either three tablets containing 500 mg calcium each,
or one tablet and two identical placebo tablets.
Commencement of calcium supplementation
Calcium versus placebo
•
Belizan 1983 commenced the trial regimen at 15 weeks'
gestation. They included women below and at 20 weeks'
gestation. The average age was 20.8 weeks in both groups.
•
Crowther 1999 included women with a gestational age less than
24 weeks; the average gestational age was 19 weeks in the
calcium group and 18 weeks in the placebo group.
•
Goldberg 2013 randomised women at 20 weeks' gestation
and the intervention started, on average, at 20.5 (± 3) weeks'
gestation in the calcium group and 20.2 (± 3) weeks' gestation in
the placebo group.
•
Levine 1997, another large trial, included women between 11
and 22 weeks' gestation. The average gestational age at baseline
in the calcium and placebo groups was 17.2 and 17.1 weeks,
respectively.
•
Villar 1987 randomised women at 26 weeks of gestation.
•
Villar 1990 included women with an average gestational age of
23.7 (± 4.3) weeks' gestation in the calcium group and 23.4 (± 3.8)
weeks' gestation in the placebo group.
•
Villar 2006, a large trial, included 8325 women before 20 weeks'
gestation. Data provided by the trial authors show that women
started the trial regimen from as early as five weeks' gestation,
with 3070 of the 8325 women (36.88%) beginning the trial
regimen before 14 weeks' gestation. Only three women were
recruited afer 20 weeks' gestation.
Low-dose versus high-dose calcium
•
The eligibility criteria of the two trials that compared low-
and high-dose calcium determined that all participants were
at or below 20 weeks' gestation (Dwarkanath (India) 2024;
Dwarkanath (Tanzania) 2024). In both these trials, more than
two-thirds of the participants began the trial regimen before 17
weeks' gestation, with approximately one-third of the total trial
sample having already started the trial regimen before 13 weeks'
gestation.
All studies continued with their specific trial regimen until delivery.
Contact with trial authors
We emailed the corresponding authors of all eligible trials to
request additional information or verification of information. None
of the authors of the trials remaining in awaiting classification had
responded to these e-mails by the time of submission.
We received unpublished information from authors of six of the
included trials, which we took in good faith and used in the review
(Belizan 1983; Belizan 1991; Crowther 1999; Dwarkanath (India)
2024; Dwarkanath (Tanzania) 2024; Goldberg 2013).
Excluded studies
We assessed five studies included in the 2018 review as ineligible

Pre-eclampsia
We judged five of the six trials included in the analysis to be at low
risk of bias in every RoB 2 domain and therefore to be at low risk of
bias overall (Belizan 1983; Crowther 1999; Levine 1997; Villar 1990;
Villar 2006).
In the remaining study, the overall risk-of-bias judgement for
pre-eclampsia is 'some concerns' (Goldberg 2013). This trial
randomised participants by colour coding, so it is unclear how
allocation was concealed, resulting in a judgement of 'some
concerns' for the domain, Bias arising from the randomisation
process.
Maternal death
We judged two of the three studies included in the analysis to be at
low risk of bias in every RoB 2 domain and therefore at overall low
risk of bias (Crowther 1999; Villar 2006).
We deemed the remaining study to have 'some concerns' overall.
Goldberg 2013 used colour-coded containers for allocation, leading
to concerns about allocation concealment and a judgement
of 'some concerns' for the domain, Bias arising from the

Summary of main results
Calcium supplementation versus placebo
Analysis 
of 
all 
included 
studies 
shows 
that 
calcium
supplementation given during pregnancy may result in little to
no diference in pre-eclampsia compared to placebo. For this
outcome, there is some heterogeneity, likely due to small-study
efects and publication bias. We performed a sensitivity analysis
excluding studies with fewer than 500 participants, and found
that there is high-certainty evidence that calcium supplementation
during pregnancy results in little to no diference in the prevention
of pre-eclampsia compared to placebo.
The evidence is very uncertain about the efect of calcium
supplementation on maternal death, adverse efects, and neonatal
death. Maternal death (5 vs 15 per 10,000 women) was too rare
for meaningful comparison. Calcium supplementation probably
results in little to no diference in the composite outcome of
maternal death or severe morbidity.
Calcium supplementation may result in little to no diference in
perinatal loss and likely results in little to no diference in stillbirth.
The evidence is very uncertain about the efect of calcium
supplementation on preterm delivery before 37 weeks when
all studies are included, but a sensitivity analysis excluding
studies with fewer than 500 participants showed that calcium
supplementation results in little to no diference in this outcome.
No trials measured the composite outcome of neonatal death or
severe morbidity.
There was no diference in these findings when we compared
women with a high versus a low baseline calcium intake. Similarly,
we did not note any diference in these findings when we compared

Low-dose versus high-dose calcium supplementation
Low-dose calcium supplementation may result in little to no
diference in pre-eclampsia compared to high-dose calcium
supplementation. The evidence is very uncertain about the efect
of low-dose calcium supplementation on maternal death. No trials
measured a composite outcome of maternal death or severe
morbidity, neonatal death or severe morbidity, or adverse events in
mothers. Low-dose calcium supplementation results in little to no
diference in perinatal loss or stillbirth, and likely results in little to
no diference in preterm delivery before 37 weeks.
Both studies in this comparison included women at high risk for
pre-eclampsia in low calcium-intake populations, so we could not
perform any subgroup analyses.
Limitations of the evidence included in the review
Our review aimed specifically to assess whether calcium is efective
for preventing pre-eclampsia.
We performed subgroup analysis of women receiving high
versus low intake of dietary calcium and this analysis did not
show a diference in preventing pre-eclampsia. However, we do
acknowledge that inequity in access to a high calcium diet exists
globally, and our review does not suggest that this inequity should
not be addressed.
There are concerns about potential publication bias in this field,
as many small studies yielded very large efects, while larger
trials did not. This may indicate that small studies with negative
results may be less likely to be published. There are also concerns
about the efect of small trials on the overall efect of calcium
supplementation [26, 166]. As we could not find a definition of
'small study' in the literature, we contacted biostatisticians and
discussed it within our author team. As a result, we defined a small
study as a trial with fewer than 500 participants, and performed
sensitivity analyses for our critical and important outcomes.
Many studies included a combination of interventions. We excluded
these studies as we were uncertain of the true efects of calcium
supplementation.
Compliance with the intervention regimen varied across the
included studies, ranging from 64% to 99%. It is thus worth noting
that treatment compliance may afect the results of these studies.
We judged nine of the included trials to have a low overall risk
of bias (Belizan 1983; Belizan 1991; Crowther 1999; Dwarkanath
(India) 2024; Dwarkanath (Tanzania) 2024; Levine 1997; Villar
1987; Villar 1990; Villar 2006). We judged one study as
'some concerns' (Goldberg 2013). During certainty of evidence
assessments using the GRADE approach, the most common reason
for downgrading evidence was imprecision, when there were very
few events (fewer than 30) and if the confidence interval around the
risk ratio was very wide.
As indicated in Certainty of the evidence assessment, the threshold
for suggested appreciable benefit for the relative efect was 0.75,
and the threshold for suggested appreciable harm was 1.25. Where
the confidence interval crossed these thresholds, we downgraded
the certainty of evidence by one, two, or three levels depending
on the width of the confidence interval and included reasons for
imprecision judgements in the footnotes of Summary of findings 1
and Summary of findings 2.

Agreements and disagreements with other studies or
reviews
Of the 27 studies included in the previous review version, we
included seven studies and excluded 11, because our eligibility
criteria have changed since the last version was published in 2018.
We recategorised nine studies as 'awaiting classification' due to our
trustworthiness assessment.
Previous reviews on this topic did not include trustworthiness
assessments, sensitivity analyses for small-study efects, and
updated methodology, which influenced the interpretation of the
results. A recent non-Cochrane review [166], and the previous
version of this Cochrane review [26], highlighted the problem with
publication bias and small-study efects. The previous version of
this Cochrane review concluded that calcium supplementation had
an efect on women with inadequate calcium in their diet. This
updated review, which includes trustworthiness assessments and
sensitivity analyses to mitigate small-study efects, now shows little
to no diference in all critical and important outcomes regardless of
calcium intake.

The maternal composite outcome in this review included data from
only one study (Villar 2006). We used a Delphi consensus on adverse
outcomes in pre-eclampsia to define the composite outcomes,
which we prespecified in our protocol [36]. We extracted outcomes
from data provided by the trial authors. Our composite outcome,
therefore, difered from the composite outcomes reported in
Villar 2006, which were not prespecified in their trial protocol.
Their first binary summary indicator, which was named 'severe
pre-eclampsia complications index', included severe gestational
hypertension and pre-eclampsia diagnosed before 32 weeks, which
were not included in our predefined composite outcome. Their
second summary indicator, which was defined as 'severe maternal
morbidity and mortality index', included maternal admission to
an intensive care unit or any special care unit. This was also not
included in our predefined composite. In the previous version of
this review, four included studies reported on this outcome, but
three of these reported no events. Only one study provided data for
the analysis (Villar 2006). They defined this outcome 'as defined by
trial authors', where we have used the definition explained above.
We are aware that an individual patient analysis is being conducted,
but the results have not yet been published.

Implications for practice
Calcium supplementation compared to placebo
Calcium supplementation compared to placebo may result in little
to no diference in pre-eclampsia, and we are very uncertain about
the efect of calcium supplementation on preterm delivery before
37 weeks. We explored concerns about small study efects and
publication bias through sensitivity analyses. When considering
only large trials (involving over 95% of participants included in
the main analyses), there is high-certainty evidence that calcium
supplementation compared to placebo results in little to no
diference in pre-eclampsia and preterm delivery before 37 weeks.
The evidence related to maternal death is very uncertain, as this
was a rare event.
Calcium supplementation compared to placebo probably results in
little to no diference in the composite outcome of maternal death
or severe morbidity, may result in little to no diference in perinatal
loss, and probably results in little to no diference in stillbirth. The
evidence is very uncertain about the efects on adverse efects and
neonatal death.
None of the included studies measured the composite outcome of
neonatal death or severe morbidity.
Baseline calcium intake level and pre-eclampsia risk status did not
impact our findings.
Low-dose compared to high-dose calcium supplementation
There was no diference with low-dose compared to high-
dose calcium supplementation in outcomes in women at high
risk for pre-eclampsia in low calcium-intake populations. Low-
dose compared to high-dose calcium supplementation during
pregnancy may result in little to no diference in pre-eclampsia.
Maternal death (5 per 10,000 women in both groups) was rare,
and the evidence is very uncertain. Low-dose compared to high-
dose calcium results in little to no diference in perinatal loss or
stillbirth and probably results in little to no diference in preterm
delivery before 37 weeks. Severe maternal morbidity, neonatal
death, severe neonatal morbidity, and adverse efects were not
measured.
Implications for research
A sensitivity analysis that included only large trials with more
than 500 participants, provides high-certainty evidence that
calcium supplementation compared to placebo makes little to no
diference in pre-eclampsia when commenced between 5 and 26
weeks of pregnancy. It is very unlikely that further high-quality,
large randomised controlled trials would change the current
evidence. Therefore, it may be more cost-efective to explore
other interventions or strategies related to the prevention of
hypertensive disorders during pregnancy.
